sections.text: How 3 Prisoners Escaped Alcatraz on a Homemade Raft.
They beat the cells, the guards, and the island. But did they beat the bay?
In June 1962, Alcatraz was called escape-proof.
The prison sat about 2 kilometres from San Francisco.
Cold water and strong currents formed a natural wall.
Since the federal prison opened in 1934, every escape had failed.
But Frank Morris and brothers John and Clarence Anglin noticed weaknesses.
A fourth planner, Allen West, helped them. He would not leave that night.
Their plan was not the first. During the federal prison years, 36 men made 14 escape attempts.
Most were caught, stopped, or died. Only this attempt left three fates unresolved.
Their cells stood beside an unguarded utility corridor.
Each rear wall had a small opening below the sink.
The men used spoons and other improvised tools to widen those openings.
They covered the damage with painted cardboard during inspections.
The work was slow. But noise from music hour helped hide the scraping.
Therefore, one by one, they could slip behind the cell block.
Above the cells, they created a hidden workshop.
Guards still counted heads at night. So the men made convincing dummies.
They shaped them from soap, paper, concrete dust, and other scraps.
Hair gathered from the prison barbershop made the trick look real.
Placed on pillows, the heads could fool a quick flashlight check.
But leaving the building was only half the problem.
They still needed to cross San Francisco Bay.
Therefore, they collected more than 50 rubberized raincoats.
They joined the seams with contact cement and heat.
The finished raft was roughly 6 feet wide and 14 feet long.
More raincoat material became life vests.
They also built a hand-operated pump to inflate everything at the shore.
Wooden paddles completed their unlikely boat.
The preparation took months, and every inspection could have ended it.
Then came the night of June 11, 1962.
The dummies took their places. The men slipped through the wall openings.
They climbed the utility space and reached the roof.
But the prison was still active around them.
They crossed rooftops, climbed down, and moved toward the island's northeast shore.
At the water, they inflated the raft and life vests.
Investigators believed their planned destination was Angel Island to the north.
The distance looked short. But the bay did not move in straight lines.
Tides could sweep a small raft toward the Golden Gate and the Pacific.
Therefore, timing mattered as much as the raft.
Sometime after 10 p.m., the three men disappeared into the dark.
For hours, guards saw quiet shapes beneath blankets.
But the morning count finally exposed the dummies.
Alcatraz locked down, boats searched the water, and aircraft scanned the bay.
Investigators found pieces of evidence, but not the three men.
A paddle was recovered, along with raincoat material and personal items.
No body was conclusively identified as Morris or either Anglin brother.
The FBI examined sightings, family contacts, and claims for 17 years.
In 1979, it closed its investigation.
The bureau's conclusion was that the men most likely drowned.
The water was cold, the current dangerous, and survival uncertain.
But likely is not the same as proven.
No verified trace showed the men alive after that night.
Yet no final physical evidence proved all three died.
Therefore, the U.S. Marshals Service continued following credible leads.
Popular culture turned the escape into a legend.
The real achievement was less glamorous: patient work, observation, and coordination.
Allen West's part also reveals how narrow the timing was.
He could not get through his opening in time.
So Morris and the Anglins left without him.
That shows the plan's strange balance. It needed teamwork, but one delay could separate the team.
Every hidden opening also had to look normal before each inspection.
Therefore, the men rehearsed inside the same strict routine they were trying to defeat.
After the alarm, each recovered object mattered because the raft itself did not provide a clear ending.
Reports appeared from across the country. But a report is not proof without a verified trail.
Investigators found no confirmed message, purchase, or family contact that settled the case.
The surviving evidence could explain how they left. It could not prove where they finished.
Even modern tide models show why simple guesses are risky.
A small change in launch time can send a floating object toward a different shore.
That means a crossing may have been possible. It does not mean this crossing succeeded.
That choice split the story into two separate questions.
Did they escape the prison building? Yes.
Did they reach lasting freedom? Nobody can prove it.
That is the key to the Alcatraz mystery.
The homemade raft solved the prison's last designed barrier.
But the bay created a final test with no confirmed answer.
The three men vanished between a proven escape and an unproven survival.
Therefore, the plan is remembered not because we know the ending.
It is remembered because every known clue stops before the ending.
History sometimes gives us an escape route, but not a destination.
